newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls along with stocks and bonds.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls along with stocks and bonds.

text.p: The dollar dropped sharply Wednesday, falling victim to a steep decline in stocks and bonds as a nervous Wall Street questioned whether its record-breaking run was faltering, currency dealers said.
Wednesday's broad sell-off revived fears that gripped the markets last week after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan made cautionary comments about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
Foreign currency dealers said Wednesday's trade in the dollar against most European currencies mirrored movements in the Dow Jones industrial average.

"Almost all of the dollar trade activity tracked the Dow. Even when the Dow tried to stage a small recovery this afternoon, the dollar followed suit," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.

The dollar touched a low of 1.5342 German marks in early trading after closing Tuesday at 1.5530 marks and staged an abortive attempt to recapture the important 1.54-mark level in the early afternoon. The dollar closed at 1.5380 marks.
Against the Japanese yen, the dollar steadily inched lower to end at 112.96 yen from 113.37 at Tuesday's close.
The Dow opened off sharply, dropping nearly 120 points by midmorning. Stocks tried but failed to pare early losses until late in the session.
The Dow recouped some of its losses to end down 70.73 points at 6,402.52. Treasury bonds also suffered heavy losses, dropping more than 1-3/4 points.
"There was no question once the asset market opened the way it did, the dollar was going to trade lower," said Bob Near, a vice president at Bank of New York.
"The drop just underscores the fact that the markets are extremely skittish in the wake of Greenspan's comments on Thursday."
Traders have fretted that the Dow, which has advanced by nearly a third this year, could be headed for a major correction.

Market jitters started in Asian and European markets due to a column in The Wall Street Journal which questioned whether Japanese financial institutions were losing interest in U.S. Treasury securities.
Several large investors later bought Swiss francs for marks and dollars, putting additional pressure on the U.S. currency.

The dollar also suffered as dealers flocked to the yen and sold the Australian dollar following a Reserve Bank of Australia interest rate cut to 6 percent from 6.5 percent. Some dealers interpreted the rate cut as a signal Australian officials wanted their currency lower.
Despite Wednesday's drop in the dollar, dealers remained optimistic that the currency's recent rally against most European currencies would soon resume.
"The long-run view, according to technical analysts and others, is that the dollar should go up and that has not really changed," said Hans Boman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank in New York.

In other trading, the dollar closed lower at 1.3108 Swiss franc compared to 1.3267 Swiss francs at Tuesday's close, but rose to Canadian $1.3610 from $C1.3585. The British pound fell to $1.6515 from $1.6540.
